extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and educated readers interested in literary composition and moral essays (18th-century literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging moral essays and epic poetry (exemplified by commentary on Paradise Lost), with advice on authorial conduct toward critics. Emphasises diction, character-portrayal, allegory use, fidelity to sources, and moral effects on readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbearance in responding to critics
rubrics_metrics.description: I have been very often tempted to write Invectives upon those who have detracted from my Works... I look upon it as a particular Happiness, that I have always hindred my Resentments from proceeding to this extremity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress satirical replies and lampoons rather than publish them; there is 'particular Merit' and 'something Great and Heroical' in letting fall instruments of revenge and stifling resentments. Personal retaliations would make a public work of little use by filling it with private reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine reproach and respond by reform or indifference (Epictetus rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does a Man reproach thee for being Proud or Ill-natured... Consider whether his Reproaches are true; if they are not, consider that thou art not the Person whom he reproaches... If his Reproaches are true... become mild, affable and obliging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticised, first examine whether the criticism is true. If false, treat it as misdirected and be at peace; if true, correct your conduct rather than engage in revenge. This is practical fortitude necessary for public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fill public works with personal reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Work would have been of very little use to the Publick, had it been filled with personal Reflections and Debates; for which Reason I have never once turned out of my way to observe those little Cavils...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting personal disputes or responses to detractors dominate public writing; keep the work focused on public usefulness and general interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of persons in epic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tenth Book of Paradise Lost has a greater variety of Persons in it than any other in the whole Poem... celestial, infernal, human, and imaginary Persons, who have their respective Parts allotted in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic benefits from a rich cast spanning divine, infernal, human, and allegorical figures, each given appropriate parts and treatment to enrich the poem's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding unity akin to a tragedy's last act
rubrics_metrics.description: It is like the last Act of a well-written Tragedy, in which all who had a part in it are generally drawn up before the Audience, and represented under those Circumstances in which the Determination of the Action places them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The closing book/act should gather principal characters and show how the action has affected each, providing a satisfactory termination and moral/account of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to scriptural language when using Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: He has rather chosen to neglect the Numerousness of his Verse, than to deviate from those Speeches which are recorded on this great occasion... has kept religiously to the Form of Words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing upon sacred texts, maintain the form and key phrases of Scripture where appropriate; fidelity to authoritative sources can be poetically valuable even at the expense of prolixity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weave poetic allusions to Scripture with beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Tho the Author in the whole Course of his Poem... has infinite Allusions to Places of Scripture, I have only taken notice... of such as are of a Poetical Nature, and which are woven with great Beauty into the Body of this Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scriptural allusions as poetical material, integrating them artfully so they enhance the fable and produce poetical effects rather than merely pedantic citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ sublime imagination for cosmic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: they are represented as infecting the Stars and Planets with malignant Influences, weakning the Light of the Sun, bringing down the Winter into the milder Regions... The following Lines... in which we see the Angels heaving up the Earth... is conceived with that sublime Imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime, large-scale imagery (cosmic, elemental transformations) is appropriate in epic contexts to convey the magnitude of moral or metaphysical events and should be conceived with imaginative grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gradual transformation and surprising episodes for infernal scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual Change of Satan himself is describ'd after Ovid's manner... The unexpected Hiss which rises in this Episode... the annual Change which they are supposed to suffer, are Instances of this kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformative, surprising episodes (borrowed from metamorphosis traditions) can delight readers; refine 'hints' and give finishing touches to make such scenes effective and astonishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful diction and judicious contrivance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beauty of the Diction is very remarkable in this whole Episode, as I have observed... the great Judgment with which it was contriv'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words with care and contrive incidents with sound judgment; diction and construction are central to producing the intended poetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize protagonists by presenting faults as frailty
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's Art is no where more shewn than in his conducting the Parts of these our first Parents... his Crime proceeds from a Weakness which every Man is inclined to pardon and commiserate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying human characters who commit wrongs, present their faults as human frailty or excessive love so readers feel pity and compassion rather than mere condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ the 'tender' (tenderness) to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton has by this means filled a great part of his Poem with that kind of Writing which the French Criticks call the Tender, and which is in a particular manner engaging to all sorts of Readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tender, compassionate passages—evoking pity and sympathy—broaden a poem's appeal; cultivate sincere emotional moments to move readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show internal moral struggle and paternal concern
rubrics_metrics.description: He immediately after recovers from his Presumption, owns his Doom to be just, and begs that the Death which is threatned him may be inflicted on him... He shows generous Concern which our first Father shews in it for his Posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict inward remorse, conscience, and concern for offspring/posterity to add moral depth and to make characters' suffering ethically resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegorical/imaginary persons sparingly in heroic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Such beautiful extended Allegories are certainly some of the finest Compositions of Genius: but... are not agreeable to the Nature of an Heroick Poem. This of Sin and Death is very exquisite in its Kind, if not considered as a Part of such a Work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, poetic personifications are effective, but extended allegorical figures that take central, continuous roles are less fitting for heroic/epic poems; limit their dramatic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification as brief poetical phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer... makes use of other such Allegorical Persons, it is only in short Expressions, which convey an ordinary Thought to the Mind in the most pleasing manner, and may rather be look'd upon as Poetical Phrases than Allegorical Descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise personifications that serve as vivid poetic shorthand (e.g., 'Victory sat on the right hand') rather than sustained allegorical narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose apt words and phrases for allegorical action
rubrics_metrics.description: a Reader who knows the Strength of the English Tongue, will be amazed to think how the Poet could find such apt Words and Phrases to describe the Action[s] of those two imaginary Persons
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing allegory or personified abstractions, select language precisely suited to the imagined actions so the expression seems inevitable and striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral messaging should favour endurance over despair
rubrics_metrics.description: The Resolution of dying to end our Miseries, does not shew such a degree of Magnanimity as a Resolution to bear them, and submit to the Dispensations of Providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When imparting moral lessons through characters' responses to suffering, valorize patience and endurance within Providence rather than praising escape via death or despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray ostentation in piety as undermining true sanctity
rubrics_metrics.description: This ostentatious Behaviour is such an Offence to true Sanctity, that it disparages it, and makes Virtue not only unamiable, but also ridiculous... a Devotée is so far from promoting Goodness, that she deters others by her Example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting religious characters, show how ostentation and performative devotion make virtue ridiculous and can deter others; distinguish genuine piety from theatrical devotion in characterization.
